title: It’s Not Just the US with High Interest Rates | Dimensional
gist: Dimensional's Wes Crill argues the rise in US Treasury yields is part of a global sovereign-yield uptrend, with Japan and France seeing larger increases since January 2025, so the data does not show US bonds losing relative desirability. Volatility-averse investors can shorten duration while natural long-bond holders can lock in higher long-end rates.

insights.claim: Interest rates have been rising for most major sovereign bond issuers in recent years, so the rise in US Treasury yields is part of a global trend rather than a US-specific phenomenon.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Frames US yield moves as global, reducing the case for a US-specific fiscal risk premium trade.

themes.theme: Supply-demand read of US bond desirability

insights.claim: Bond yields are set by supply and demand: when supply rises relative to demand, yields must rise to attract additional capital.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Heavy sovereign issuance globally implies upward pressure on yields independent of country-specific credit concerns.
insights.quote: When supply increases versus demand, yields must go up to attract additional capital.
insights.locator: Bond yields are influenced by supply and demand

insights.claim: Cross-country 30-year sovereign yield data from September 2021 to September 2026 does not indicate that US bonds are losing desirability relative to other countries' bonds.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Undercuts the thesis of foreign demand abandoning Treasuries; dollar-asset exodus not visible in relative yields.
insights.quote: The global yield data doesn’t make a case that US bonds are waning in desirability versus those of other countries.
insights.locator: Bond yields are influenced by supply and demand

insights.claim: Investors worried about bond volatility can shift to shorter-duration portfolios, which suffer smaller price impacts from rate changes, rather than chasing yield.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Suggests a barbell by investor type: volatility-sensitive capital shortens duration.
insights.quote: Investors who are concerned about bond volatility may wish to allocate to shorter duration portfolios
insights.locator: This is not to say everyone

insights.claim: Natural holders of long-dated bonds who are less sensitive to rate movements, such as liability-matching investors, can benefit from the higher yields now available on long bonds.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Elevated long-end yields are an opportunity for liability-driven and buy-and-hold investors to lock in rates.
insights.quote: The natural holders of long-dated bonds, who may be less sensitive to the impact of rate movements, can enjoy the higher rates
